description: HEXAFIRE is a team of six engineers specialized in Stochastic Modeling, Statistics and Finance, Numerical Modeling and Simulation, and Computer Science and Operations Research. We combine data analysis, mathematical modeling, computational methods, and problem-solving skills to develop innovative solutions. We are really interested in using NASA Earth observation data to improve the detection, analysis, and understanding of wildfire hotspots. We value creativity, collaboration, and rigor.
summary: HEXAFIRE is a web application that turns 25 years of NASA active-fire detections into one consistent monthly fire calendar for any area. MODIS has observed fires since 2000 but is being replaced by VIIRS, whose finer pixels detect about six times more hotspots by day and fifteen times more at night. Joining the two records creates a false rise in fire activity. We express VIIRS in MODIS units. For each 0.25° cell, we compute how often each satellite passed over it, then estimate the sensitivity gap from 2012–2020, when both sensors flew together, separately for each region, calendar month, day and night. On an interactive globe, users pick a country, a place or draw an area, and get a plain-language summary, a calendar from November 2000 to today, each month’s departure from its 2003–2020 normal, a comparison of two areas or two years, and downloads. We tested the challenge’s own goal: the sensor of origin must not change the verdict on a month. Over 2012–2020, converted VIIRS agrees with real MODIS with Cohen’s kappa = 0.747 (0.558 for a single global factor), and false anomalies fall from 24% to 9%. Fire managers can compare the current season with two decades of history without a satellite change triggering false alarms.
details:
Live app: https://sergedmds.github.io/HEXA_FIRE/
Code and documents: https://github.com/Sergedmds/HEXA_FIRE/

What it does

HEXAFIRE gives any area on Earth a consistent calendar of fire activity from November 2000 to today. It combines NASA's MODIS record (Terra and Aqua, since 2000) with the newer VIIRS record (Suomi NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21, since 2012). In the harmonized series, a change of satellite no longer looks like a change in fire activity.

The user chooses an area (box, polygon, point with radius, country or place search) and a date range, then gets:

  • A plain-language summary: when fires usually peak in the area, whether the latest month was above or below usual, and how the last complete year ranks.
  • A year × month calendar of harmonized hotspot counts, or of each month’s departure from its 2003–2020 normal, with explanations of what a hotspot is and how to read the colours.
  • Details on hover: the value of the month, its 95% interval, the raw detections, the normal for that month and the mean fire radiative power (FRP).
  • Three key figures: latest month available, its departure from normal, and the usual peak month.
  • The monthly layer: harmonized hotspots or departure from normal on a 1° grid over the globe, with a month slider and an animation.
  • Built-in proof: the raw record next to the harmonized one, with the 95% uncertainty band of converted months, and the validation results.
  • Compare: two areas or two years side by side, summarized in a few sentences.
  • About & guide: what the site shows, key terms, what it does and does not do, in plain words.
  • Downloads: calendar as CSV, JSON, PNG and SVG, a CSV of all 0.25° cells of the area month by month, and a shareable link

How it works

A Python engine processes the NASA monthly active fire archives offline, then publishes light files read directly by the browser.

  • Preparation: Vegetation fires only, MODIS confidence ≥ 30, VIIRS "low" confidence removed. Detections are counted per 0.25° cell, month, and day or night.
  • Same number of looks: For each cell, the engine computes how many times each satellite passed over it in the month, from latitude, swath width and orbit, and removes the days without data.
  • Conversion: From 2012 to 2020, MODIS and Suomi NPP observed together. For a cell-month seen by both, the VIIRS share of the combined count follows a binomial law whose logit equals the sensitivity gap plus the log ratio of overpasses. The true fire activity cancels out. The gap is estimated by maximum likelihood for each 10° region, calendar month and period (day or night). Estimates from sparse regions are shrunk towards their regional average (DerSimonian–Laird).
  • One series: MODIS stays as measured until December 2020. Converted VIIRS takes over in January 2021, before the orbital drift of Terra and Aqua. Suomi NPP is converted directly; NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 are linked to it by the same method when their overlap is available. Several VIIRS satellites are averaged, never added.
  • Labels and uncertainty: Every month is marked as measured, converted, provisional or partially covered. Every converted value carries a 95% interval from the uncertainty of the conversion.

Does it work?

The challenge asks that the sensor of origin no longer matter, so we tested exactly that. For each year from 2012 to 2020, the conversion was fitted without that year, VIIRS was converted as if MODIS no longer existed, and each region-month received a verdict (low, normal or high). This verdict was compared with the one given by real MODIS, over 17,309 region-months.

  • HEXAFIRE: Cohen's kappa 0.747, false anomalies 9.0%, median error 0.125.
  • A single global factor: kappa 0.558, false anomalies 23.9%, median error 0.262.
  • Raw VIIRS: kappa 0.014, false anomalies 92.1%.

The 95% interval of the kappa gain over the global factor is [0.174, 0.205]. Fourteen automated tests check the engine, including recovering a known conversion factor from simulated data.

Benefits

  • One unit across 25 years, so trends and anomalies are no longer sensor artefacts.
  • Honest status labels: a month without detections is never shown as a month without fire, and converted values are marked.
  • Built-in proof: the validation and the raw versus harmonized comparison are inside the application.
  • Free and light: a static website with no server, no account and no installation. It opens on a phone, in English or French.

Expected impact

Early-warning and emergency services can check in seconds whether this month is unusual for their area, without a false alarm caused by the change of satellite. Land managers and firefighters can see when their area usually burns and which years were exceptional. Scientists get a single series instead of two incompatible ones, at the time MODIS is being retired. For fire-prone regions such as West Africa, where much burning is agricultural and pastoral, it puts two decades of NASA data in the hands of local services at no cost.

Tools used

  • Engine: Python 3.12 with pandas, NumPy, PyArrow and pytest.
  • Web application: HTML, CSS and JavaScript without a build step, MapLibre GL JS for the interactive globe, and hand-written SVG charts.
  • Data and hosting: lftp to download the monthly archives, the NASA FIRMS API integrated in the engine for months after the latest archive, GitHub and GitHub Pages.
  • Documentation: LaTeX.
  • Design: page mockups generated with Google Stitch (SI); globe background from NASA GIBS.
  • SI assistance: Claude (Anthropic) for code, research and writing, and Google Stitch for the mockups, as described in the “Use of SI tools” section of the README.

What makes it creative

  • We judge the method by the challenge's own goal
    Rather than claiming to recover the true number of fires, which no one can verify, we test whether the verdict on a month stays the same when MODIS is replaced by converted VIIRS.
  • Conditioning instead of guessing. By working on the share of VIIRS in the combined count, the unknown fire activity disappears from the equations, and both sensors are treated symmetrically.
  • Two units, one meaning. Users can display MODIS-equivalent or VIIRS-equivalent values, and the departure from normal stays practically the same.

Factors we considered

  • A hotspot is not a wildfire: the application explains it under the calendar and on the About & guide page, and never states “no fire”, only “no hotspot detected”.
  • Overpasses and outages: counts are compared for the same number of satellite looks.
  • Day and night: the gap between sensors is much larger at night, so both periods are handled separately.
  • Orbital drift of Terra and Aqua: the switch to VIIRS is set before it.
  • Accessibility: colour-blind-safe palettes, and status shown by marks as well as colour.
  • Low bandwidth: data load tile by tile on demand.
  • Data terms: all NASA data are acknowledged, and their provenance and versions are documented.

Known limits, stated openly:

  • overpasses come from an analytical formula, not yet from real granule footprints;
  • regions are 10° blocks;
  • the interval covers only the conversion uncertainty;
  • the published series runs to November 2026; September to November 2026 are provisional, based on MODIS from the NASA FIRMS API.
  • the CSV gives cell-month values, not individual detections.
